source_text: Aemulari aliquem irritare etiam est et provocare. In Deuteronomio: Ipsi in zelum adduxerunt me in non Deo; et ego in zelum adducam eos. Apostolus: An aemulamur Dominum? Deus noster Deus zelans. Qui peccat Deum zelantem in zelum incitat.
thought_title: Envy as provocation of a jealous God
orientation: Origen is explaining the opening command of Psalm 36 by showing that envy is not only a feeling but an act that provokes God, who is jealous.
pass_a_gloss: To emulate someone [is] also to irritate and to provoke. In Deuteronomy: They themselves into jealousy led me in [what is] not God; and I into jealousy will lead them. [The] Apostle: Or do we emulate [the] Lord? Our God [is a] jealous God. [He] who sins [against] God [who is] jealous into jealousy incites [him].

choices.term: Aemulari aliquem irritare etiam est et provocare
choices.english: To envy someone is also to irritate and to provoke
choices.why: Keeps the three verbs distinct and preserves the explanatory force of 'etiam est' (is also), showing envy as an active provocation.
rejected: To envy someone also means to irritate and provoke
Envy of someone is also irritation and provocation

choices.term: Ipsi in zelum adduxerunt me in non Deo
choices.english: They themselves brought me into jealousy with what is not God
choices.why: Renders 'ipsi' as emphatic 'themselves' and keeps the awkward 'in non Deo' literally as 'with what is not God' to preserve the Septuagint phrasing Origen quotes.
rejected: They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god
They made me jealous with a non-god

choices.english: Or do we envy the Lord?
choices.why: Keeps the interrogative particle 'An' as 'Or' and the present tense 'aemulamur' as 'do we envy', matching the rhetorical question form.
rejected: Are we envious of the Lord?
Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?

choices.english: Our God is a jealous God
choices.why: Preserves the noun repetition 'Deus...Deus' and renders 'zelans' as 'jealous' per the glossary sense of provoking God to jealousy.
rejected: Our God is a zealous God
Our God is a God who is jealous

choices.term: Qui peccat Deum zelantem in zelum incitat
choices.english: The one who sins incites the jealous God into jealousy
choices.why: Keeps the participle 'zelantem' as 'jealous' and the phrase 'in zelum' literally as 'into jealousy', preserving the causal chain Origen draws.
rejected: Whoever sins provokes the jealous God to jealousy
The sinner stirs the jealous God to jealousy

bible_refs.note: Ipsi in zelum adduxerunt me in non Deo; et ego in zelum adducam eos

pass_b_english: To envy someone is also to irritate and to provoke. In Deuteronomy it says: They themselves brought me into jealousy with what is not God, and I will bring them into jealousy (Deuteronomy 32:21). The Apostle asks: Or do we envy the Lord? (1 Corinthians 10:22). Our God is a jealous God (Exodus 20:5). The one who sins incites the jealous God into jealousy.

last_rejected.quote: Or do we envy the Lord?
last_rejected.why: Rhetorical question flattened to statement; Paul challenges, doesn't ask neutrally.
last_rejected.fix: Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy?
last_rejected.ruling: English says 'asks' and uses '?', preserving the rhetorical question. No flattening to statement occurred.
